title: Hermann Weyl
wiki_lead:
Hermann Klaus Hugo Weyl ( VILE; German: [vaɪl]; 9 November 1885 – 8 December 1955) was a German mathematician, theoretical physicist, logician and philosopher. He was one of the most influential mathematicians of the twentieth century. Although much of his working life was spent in Zürich, Switzerland, and then Princeton, New Jersey, he is associated with the University of Göttingen tradition of mathematics, represented by Carl Friedrich Gauss, David Hilbert and Hermann Minkowski.
Weyl made significant contributions to an exceptionally wide range of intellectual fields, including mathematics, physics, philosophy and logic, with interests extending to the nature of space, time, matter and symmetry, as well as the history of mathematics. The originator of gauge theory, which became a fundamental framework of particle physics, Weyl was a pioneer in applying group theory to quantum mechanics, and made foundational contributions to many branches of mathematics such as differential geometry and number theory. He developed or introduced concepts and results such as gauge invariance, the Peter–Weyl theorem, equidistribution theorem and the Weyl law. 
He was one of the first to conceive of combining general relativity with the laws of electromagnetism. In cosmology, he theoretically derived the linear redshift–distance relation later known as Hubble's redshift law, several years before Hubble's observations. 
An important member of the Institute for Advanced Study during its early years, Weyl conceived of mathematics as an organic whole, a view informed by his philosophical outlook, and this conception shaped his work across disciplines. Freeman Dyson wrote that Weyl alone bore comparison with the "last great universal mathematicians of the nineteenth century", Henri Poincaré and David Hilbert. Vladimir Arnold and Aleksei Parshin said that his mathematical, philosophical, physical and literary breadth made him “a phenomenon of twentieth-century German culture in entirety".

Biography
Hermann Weyl was born in Elmshorn, a small town near Hamburg, in Germany, and attended the Gymnasium Christianeum in Altona. His father, Ludwig Weyl, was a banker; whereas his mother, Anna Weyl (née Dieck), came from a wealthy family.
From 1904 to 1908, he studied mathematics and physics at both the University of Göttingen and the Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. His doctorate was awarded at the University of Göttingen under the supervision of David Hilbert, whom he greatly admired.
In 1913, Weyl married Friederike Bertha Helene Joseph, known as Helene or Hella.

Helene had studied philosophy and mathematics at the University of Göttingen, where she attended the lectures of phenomenologist Edmund Husserl. She later became a translator of Spanish and English literature into German, particularly the works of Spanish philosopher José Ortega y Gasset. Helene's studies under Husserl seem to have helped stimulate Weyl's interest in phenomenology, although Weyl had himself attended Husserl's lectures during his student years in Göttingen. Weyl and Helene had two sons, Fritz Joachim Weyl and Michael Weyl, both of whom were born in Zürich, Switzerland. Helene died in Princeton, New Jersey, on 5 September 1948. A memorial service in her honor was held in Princeton on 9 September 1948. Speakers at her memorial service included her son Fritz Joachim Weyl and mathematicians Oswald Veblen and Richard Courant. In 1950, Weyl married sculptor Ellen Bär (née Lohnstein), who was the widow of professor Richard Josef Bär of Zürich.
After taking a teaching post for a few years, Weyl left Göttingen in 1913 for Zurich to take the chair of mathematics. There he overlapped with Albert Einstein, who, together with Marcel Grossmann, was working on the mathematical formulation of general relativity.
